div.head: SUMMER RAMBLES ROUND MANCHES.
div.p: SUMMER RAMBLES ROUND MANCHES.
TER. 'SALTON CASTLE.

The Manchester Guardian" of Tuesday gives a view of Ilalton Castle, by Mr. Alfred Rimmer, together with the following account Halton , Castle, like Beeston, is situated on the top of a conical hill, and commands views of exceeding beauty. These castles both suffered during the Civil Mars, and indeed their ruins areamong the many inheritances that we owe to the House of St tart. The early history of I tattoo Castle is extremely interesting. Hugh Loma, Earl of Chester in the Conqueror's thee, conferred the manor upon his cousin Nigel. Ile invested him also with great timers. lie made him Constable of Chester, and he made him his marshal. so that he should lead the van of the army whenever he undertook an invasion lof Wales. The barony of Halton continued in the family until it reverted by. marriage to John Lacy, , who afterwards became Earl of Lincoln. Alice, who was the daughter and sole heireas of Henry Lacy, Earl of Lincoln, married Thomas Plantagenet, Earl I of Lancaster, from whom &wended John of Gaunt, , Duke of Lancaster. Ile made Halton his favourite 'residence, and used it no a hunting seat. During ' his time and for many reiterations afterwards there s‘ sane part of England which was totter supplied , with game than Cheshire. The woods of Helm more and the retreats of Wales were secure hiding- ,' places for larger game, such as red .lecr and wolves, I and the great marshes mot ..avelhanks of the , estuary of the Mersey opposite Halton were safe I retreats for wildfowl. Even now the inaccessible state of the mud banke at low water in the arm of the river makes them safe resorts for wild deck When I walked along the Halton road the other. day, two frocks of wild duck, numbering 17 and 16 , each, passed over the lane, though at a considerable height. enuntryman to whom I pointed them out said it was'not an uncommon sight, but "there , wan no getting at them." There were simple con- trivances in John ad Gaunt's time, whim they were, an Cowper makes Selkirk my on his lonely island, I "no anaemia' omed to man that their tameness was shocking to me." But even now there is a decoy for wild duck on the Hale Marshes, opposite the ' castle of Halton, and when loom it, some years ago, the keeper told me that they had taken 710 wild duck in it during the previous year. Smaller game, sueh as hares and rabbits, abounded in these parts. and the lords of Halton found the district a perfect paradise for hawking. The barony, or. aunt is called in some old records, the "honor" of Halton, reverted to the Crown as a portion of Om Duchy of Lancaster. The lords of Halton had great privileges in Chester, sueli Os. among many other rights, the °woody of the streets daring the great fair of St. Werhumh. Dur- ing the feast ol St. Werburgh the barons of Halton ' had enacted that no malefactor or felon could he arreated, whatever his misdoing* were, unless , for some new offence, and this brought a very large concourse of visitors, that might in the pre- sent day be fairly represented by the crowds that come in to the Cheater races. It no happened that Randle. Earl of Chester, was besieged in Rhuddlan , Castle by the Welsh, and he gent to Roger de Lacy for aid. This was during the great fair, and the baron of Halton gat hertvl together the delinquents and marched to the aid of Randle. When the motley grasp appeared in sight of the cmtle the besiegers fled panic stricken, and the Earl was free. Like Chester castle and some others, Halton enclosed a large cone, and we have some records of its appearance in Cromwell's time. It was tben in a ruinous condition, having been garrisoned for the King and afterwanls taken and garrisoned by the Parliamentary forces. The survey speaks of a gate- house with five moms over, and a great hall, with nine unfinished rooms, and a prison for Halton honor? In Orrnerod's Cheshire " there is ft foe-simite of an etching of Halton Castle in which the gateway is shown. It seems to have been an imposing and lofty piece of architecture. The date of the picture is not given. The landscape must have been of incomparable beauty then there were no factories, and the vapours from St. Helens and Widnes had not begun to blacken the trees. Prescot and Knowaley and Runcorn are clearly shown, and the spire of Winwick rises above the woods ; while on the rich pasture and meadows just below the castle Norton Priory appears in its old form, just as it was when converted from a monastery to a private mansion. Halton Castle was held for the Ring during the Civil War by Lord Rivers, and he appointed Walter l'rimrose, a Prod- sham man, to be the governor. Then• is no account of its having sustained a siege, and it is probable that it surrendered gnietly to Sir William Brereton, the great Parliamentary leader in Cheshire ; it was probably dismantled noon after the close of the Civil War, and at about the same time as Beeston I What architectural treasures we may have lest linen! At the Leeds Assizes on Tuesday the case in which William Barrett was accused of the murder of the boy Gill at Brantford developed a peculiar , difficulty. The Grand Jury had thrown out the bill I , against the prisoner, and Mr. Forbes said lie was instructed that it would he useless to proceed on the Coroner's inquisition. There were three courses open to the prosecution- -one of which was) to apply to the Attorney, General to enter a male prwqui. Mr. Weekly, who appeared for Barrett, urged that his client should Inc allowed to plead, nod that a ver- dict of' not guilty" upon the Coroner's warrant should Inc returned, seeing that the Grand Jury had thniwn out the Treasury bill for Printer. Mr. Com- missioner White, who was outing in the Crown Court, preferred not to give any decision as to the ' course to adopt until he had consulted Mr. Justice Denman. After consultation he felt hound to leave the Crown counsel to decide upon his own course. Mr. Waddy remark.] that he had never heard of a not& primersi aa a coroner's inquisition, and doubted whether the Attorney General had power to enter one. Ultimately Barrett was placed in the dock, and arraigned for the murder. He pleaded "not guilty." Mr. Forbes said hedid not propose to offer any evidence, the jury was directed to return a verdict of " not guilty," and Barrett was acquitted. A great crowd had gathered outside the court, no intense was the interest in the ens,. ; but the man who has been arrested, freed, re-arrested, and again liberated went quietly on his way without attract- ing their attention.

EXAMINER,
SATI'ItDAY, MARCH 18. 1889.

Tun Government are anxious that the country I should have something else to think about besides the discredit which has fallen upon them in con- nection with the collapse of the charge. against Mr. PARNELL ;cml so they are going in for a pro- posal to spend U 1,500,000 upon additions to the Navy. It in a Tory trick of the oldest kind to seek to divert attention from home affairs by engagiug in a little war, or by getting up a big war score But the country is getting familiar with the gone, and it may be played once too often. IS "lir Navy in such a lamentable condition that we really need, in a time of peace, to spend these ert to millions upon it ? That is the question at issue, and it is A question which ought to I be satisfactorily aria wered before Parliament assents to this new and heavy tax upon the corn- munity. We ore aware that it is proposed to wicalpy Immo four or five years in building the sevcnty new ships which, it is suggested, should be added to our fleet; and, further, that the payment° are to extend over at least seven years. But why, seven years ? The sound rule in finance is to pay your way as you go; and it is mischievous and delusive to defer payment in the way proposed. . I Mr. Gostmcs has alwaya posed as a strict purist in matters of finance; hut he seems to have become utterly demoralised since lie became Chancellor of Vie Exchequer in a Tory Government. Can it be that evil communications have corrupted Ids good manners ? Whatever the cause, there is no question an to his decline ; and we are glad to See that Lord Raxmn.rii CHURCHILL, who resigned office rather than be party to a policy of extravagance, is determined to assist the Oppodtion in exposing the weakness and inconsistency of the Government scheme. His lordship is well entitled to ask why, if seventy ships are needed now, reductions were made in the estimates for 18t,7 and IreAS ? It is not suggest.' that any complication in foreign affairs has sud- denly arisen to warrant a sudden addition to the Navy. On the contrary, it was stated in the Queen's Speech only the other thy that England is 4;11 friendly terms with all foreign powers. The country hae shown in the past, and is ready to slam again, its willingness, if necessary, to spend a hundred millions for the defence of the Empire ; but the need must be apparmit ; there must he better reason forthe expenditure of even Twenty nillions than the fanciful one that it suits the Tory party to make a diversion, and that it is part of their policy when in office to incur heavy , obligations, and leave their Liberal successors to pay the piper. If the Government are really, anxious to effect 1.11 improvement in military mat- ters, let them devote themselves to the task of recognising effete and extravagant departments. It is notorious, rind as scandalous as it is notorious, that our aystem,or rather lack of syntem,is so great thatvast awns of money are squandered every year through sheer mismanagement. It is suggested that Lord It. Curitenitt is opposing the Govern- ment because there has been no evidence of a desire on the part of Lord SALISBURY to re-place him in the Cabinet; but we do not see any need, in this instance, for imputing personal motives. Lord RANDOIXII would in fact he guilty of tho greenest inconsistency if he took any other course. He ftwiemed as Chancellor of the Exchequer and leader of the House of Commons rather than remain SA a member of a Ministry which would not com- mit itself to a policy of retrenchment and depart- mental reform. He hari stuck to his guns since ' that time ; and it would be in the highest degree discreditable to him if he were to display the white feather at a time when the Government not only show no signs of retrenchment, but actually rush , to the other extreme. It seems to us that the proposal of the Government is simply outrageous. We are spending the vast sum of Thirty Millions menially .111 the Army and Navy, and nearly as mob every year in paying the interest upon debts for wain in the past; and yet we are told it is not- - enough ! The answer which the country ought to ! give is that it is enough, and more than enough,! and that members of Parliament who vote for the Twenty-one Millions Bill will have to reckon with ! their constituents at the next election.

Mt. SANULL SMITH. M.P., has raised an import- ant question by the protest he hes made against the growing tendency to cater for amuse- ment at political clubs. The particular occasion which line led him to enter upon the subject is "as Invitation to attend a competition between two professional billiard players at the Reform Club, Liverpool, where stages are to be erected, while the exhiLitioil is to take place at three in the afternoon mid at eight in the evening." Mr. Sums adds : '• I feel strongly on thin subject, because I know of icony young 11011 whose careers have been ruined

by betting, a habit sometimes even contee.ted by 1,p7,31ti0.s ; and I have been again and again upon to make up defiCiollolol4 conical by robbing their masters to pay gambling In view of his remarkable experience, th.• ,lier for Flintshire is certainly justified in 'f ti emmtenance a special exhibition of t which much betting goes on." Billiards or, liot of course wrong in themselves oop it necessarily injitrious to witness • clever play by particularly clever art : but the point is whether it in advisable •-• clubs to provide amusements of tlais em•tainly agree with Mr. SMITH in say- - -n •• :,t three o'clock in the afternoon, young m attA•11111fIg to their IMAilleSSoind not • - seek exhibitions.- Their time is not • .. it is sold to their employers ; and it is of frond to attend an billiard match when tit.; ill be giving lined work iureturn for hard

IWINSFOED LEFT STRANDRD.-It wan announced in Winsford on Tuesday night that after further consideration the Cheshire Lines Company was unable to recede from its decision to close the line '1 to W' insford for passenger traffic. The inhabitants of Winsford and the loculity, numbering about 15,000, are consequently much perturbed, for the , Company's resolve will debar them from direct railway communication with Manchester, and also with Liverpool and mtny parts of North Wales. A MARRIAOR ARRANOND In COURT,- Before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie and A. C. McCorquoilale, at the Newton Pe ty S-ssistia, on Saturday, a young man named John Williams, Wits summoned to show , cause why he should not contribute to the support I of the illegitimate child of Jane Davies. Defendant admitted that Inc was the father of the child, and added that he was willing to marry the complain- ant.-The Cierk If the imagist rat ea were to adjourn the case for a month do pm think the wedding would come off between now and Ii ? (laughter) Could it a+ far as you are concerned ? --Defendant : Well, I don't know, sir. I have several linings to do; I am keeping a mother, sister and four children from the Bedford Umon.-The Clerk I That has nothing to do with this case. --Mr. A. C. Sll.Corquo- dale : It will nave ue the trontile of making an order upon you if you will marry her--Defendant : I am quite willing-Mr. Gillespie n It will be muck better for you if you are going to loamy her that theorder is not made.-- Defendant saint he would prefer the order being made. -The Clerk: We might adjourn it for two menthe. Cannot you manage this little business in the course of a month, or will it take you six weeks? -Defendant I don't know how long it will take, to tell you the truth. -Mr. If we adjourn the case for two months de you think you will marry the girl within that time ?-Defendant I might do----Mr. Gillespie But we must not have any " might do." It must be " via' or " no." -Defendant I will do, sir (Laughter).- Mr. Gillespie : Then we will adjourn Line ease for two months.-- Defendant Thanks, , -The ponies then left the. court.

cash. But it is another thing, is it not to that &Terming amusements at pditieul chdos. If the membeni wish to have. concert, or a hillier:l handi- cap, there cars be no harm in that—so hug Its care is taken to see that everything is properly conducted. Granted that " political clubs were not instituted fm such purpose., it is still true that it is the rule with institutions I:if almost all kinds to add to their original objects lit is the law of their being. The main thing is to see to it that the original objects are not lost sight of—that the old order :loth not give plaee entirely to the new. This way danger lies, and it is danger to which there is need to call attention. There is ti, denying that the Three as—becr, h,aoca, and billiards—form too promin- ent features in most of our political clubs. The animal wants are luxuriously attended to, but the intellectual prociaim is, by contrast, suggestive of Falstalfs "halfpenny worth of bread to au intoler- able deal of sack.' As there are billiard and bowling matehes, Tory clubs encountering Liberal, it semis pertinent to ask why there should not be intellectual conteats—discussions between different and differing clubs on the leading questions of the day It appears to us that thesuggestion is one which might be carried out with great advantage in imily respects. It would add a new interest to the chills o.einselves ; it would atinmlate political thought and pfilitical activity generally and what ia of no less impor- tance it would meourage amongst opponents mutual toleration and not ud respect. We frankly admit that we have found a soul of good hi the stupidest Tunes una we dare say it would be dis- covered by the:4ller side, that there is aomething not altogetiicr bad when you get t:: the heart of the most rabid Radieol. The experiment is at any rate worth making. It could it, no harm, 1m d it might take away something of the reproach which at pnwent attaches to political clubs.

LORDHARTINGTON'S speech on Wednesday even- ing in Holloway iiall, London, cannot be said to add anything new to the Home Rule controversy, or, for that matter, to indicate any change in his attitude, which is that of stolid resistance. It is interesting to observe that, whilst doing all that he can to keep the present Government in office, he still regards himself as a leader of the Liberal party. Unlike Mr. CHAMBBRLAIN, lie DlVrayB speaks respectfully of Mr. GLADSTONE, but he complains that the great Liberal leader has com- mitted himself to a programme which goes further , than the programme of 188$1. His theory would seem to be that, because Lord HA RTINGTON chOONCE to stand still, the world and Mr. GLADSTONE mud not move on. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN was certainly ! not far out of it when he spoke of his lordship as RIP VAN WINKLE, 81141 it is Mr. CHAMBRRLAIN'S bitterest punishment to-day that he cannot escape having to acknowledge that, Radical though he ' still claims to be, he bus RIP VAN Wisnox for a leader. Lord HARTINGTON makes it clear that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN does not speak for him when he puts forthhia various plans for the settlement of the Irish questiou. He says:— Some of us, of whom I admit I was one, have always doubted whether it would be possible to formulate any measure of se-called Rome Rule which should satisfy at once the wishes and the desires which were cherished by a large portion of , the Irish people, and at the same time conform to the conditions which wen, admitted to he es-ential to the continued safety and prosperity of the empire. Others, among whom was the dist inginsh- ed brother of your representative, Mr. Chamber- lain, were more ready than I was to discuss alterna- tive plans, which should grant to the Lish people a large measure of self-government, and at the same time aim at satisfying conditions which the Home Rulers, with Mr. Gladstone at their head, themselves laid down.

We gather from this that ono reason for the fail- ure of the Round Table Conference was that, how- ever far Mr. CLUMBERLAIN and Sir GEORGE THEVELAN might be disposed to go, Lori HARTINOTON wan not in the humour for moving a single step in the direction of Home Rule. That in his position to-day, and, as he has shown him- -11 self thus far consistent, it will pro lushly be his position until Home Rule is an accomplished fact. After that, it would seem that he is looking for- ward to working in anis ni with the Libor il party; and he is therefor° anxious that in the meantime it should not boom.) too Radical for him. He is not as yet prepared to move on, and ho does not like to be left behind. But he has m ado his choice, and will have to abide by it. Sad as it is to feel that so many years are boing lost, it is something to reflect that when the Liberals return to power—when the next forward movement is made—there will he such a quickening of the pace as this generation has not witnessed. Lord HAIM NOTON may lament, but it is as certain that he will be left stranded as it is certain that he is a stand-still Whig and not an advancing Liberal.

There is a story going the rounds of a diamond merchant, gone mad, who present.' a waiter on board a steamer on Lake Como with is neat little , paper packet —as a " tip." The sceptical waiter ; made out his " tip' to be bits of glass, and on getting on shore throw the gems away. And now other people are Imiking for them, while the waiter ruminates by no means happily. Moral treat gifts as well as guests reverently; you may entertain diamonds unawares.

Warringtonians take to gyinmvtics as ducks take to water. It must bus', • 11. thou could not have beaten Leicester after a few weeks practice, and cense within a turn of beating Dublin. The fact that Dahlia was all behind except Us tests where special training WM of special service, sug- gests that, after the experience of a season or two, the Warrington team will probably prove one of the most formidable in the country. More power to their elbow—and every other just.

On Monday, the men employed in the Bessemer departments of the Barrow Steel Company came out on strike. A fortnight ago the men asked for a considerable advance. The manager has offered ' to submit the gnestion to a joint committee, or to an arbitrator. This is • good sign. There was a time when proposals for arbitration came solely from the side of the men. But when employers advance in the right path, the employed must not recede. "Strike, but hear" is a good motto for both sides.

Irish officials seeni to be playing a deep game in !' connection with the murder of Inspector Martin , at Gweedore. Every person whom they " suspect of being a suspect' is "run in," the idea apparently being that if no charge can be proved against him he will at least be prevented, as a prisoner, from , giving evidence for the other side. The murder of the Inspector was a shocking thing, arising out of shocking mismaingzement: but it is making had worse to treat the peasantry of Gweedore as if ' every peasant was a murderer.

The" Times would have done' well 'to hack lout of the Parnell inquiry when Pigott confessed his forgeries; for the further it goes and the deeper it gets in the mire. On Tuesday another of its wit- nesses—one Coffey,a disreputable Irish journalist confessed that his statement to the " Times " was a puree! of lies. Ile was so impudent in the matter . that he was sent to gaol for contempt of court. He , is not being treated a whit worse than he deserves; but why, oh why, has the" Times "allowed itself to be imposed upon by the Pigotts am! Colfeys of Ire- land And Echo answers "why."

The Liberals have done wonderfully well at Barnsley to return Lord Compton with a majority 'of 2,451. It m true that the majority is 57 less than the majority of IPA° ; nut that does not signify ; the marvel is to maintain a majority of over 2,000. It is well known that, when there is a large majority to play on, certain of the voters cannot be got to the poll. People, too, away from home, whether on business or on pleasure bent, do not see the fun of hastening back to heroine part of a majority of 2,451. By-the-bye, 'where is the Barnsley Liberal Unionist ?

"Truth " says : Mr. Caine is quite right in his strictures upon the missionaries in India. As Mr. Caine has said, the feet of the salary beingadequate , for a family, and the style of life which such a salary implies, utterly destroy the utility of our missionaries. lam no particular admirer of the Salvation Army, but when I hear of a Salvation missionary in India cheerfully living on £7 per annum, and a society missionary spending about L4OO per annum dose by, leanest help contrasting the self-sacrificing zeal of the one with the luxuri- one of the other. And so, too, probably do the Hindoos.

In an article on 'Bungling a the Admiralty," the " Daily News" of yesterday says :—" Some elope, owing to the niiscalculations of their designers, have their armour wholly muter water ; others are so slow as to be almost worthless; still others, though fast in smooth water, are incapable of steaming against anything like a sea ; and many are structurally so weak that either they are imperilled by the firing of their own guns, or they may he put out of action by the fire of hostile guns of light calibre directed against their unarmoured ports." In view of such bungling, it might be of greater service to the service, if instead of providing more millions, I orders wore given to hang one of the lords of the Admiralty.

Mr. Parnell hail a magnificent reception at the great meeting which was hold in St. James's Hall, London, on Wednesday. It is stated that there was a "whirlwind of enthusiasm," and that the cheering lasted for full three minutes. Referring in his speech to the action of his enemies ho said "They have been able to humbug and hoodwink the people of this country on the Irish question with the utmost facility, and so it has happened that the Tory party, which in IY+Sii, by the mouth lof Lord Carninvon, promised an Irish Parliament I •to us, in 1886 and 1587 turned right round, renewed the policy of coercion, 21114 produced I forged letters HS proofs of the criminality of the Irish members." But the policy of "humbug and hoodwink " is on its last legs, and those legs are I carrying it to the grave.

At the Liverpool Presbytery, on Monday, a letter was read from the Rev. Joseph Forrest, of :he Presbyterian Church, Douglas, announcing his resignation because the majority of his office-bear- ers had, notwithstanding his remonstrance, atten- ded a Rams' Supper. Poor Burns ! The " unco pod" cannot forgive him for writing the" Holy Fair " and "The Kirk's Alarm " ; but they might remember UlBO that he wrote " The Cotter's Saturday Night " winch has more true piety in it- than half the sermons preached. Ministers of the Reel. Forrest type don't seem to be able to timplish between what is worst in a man and what is best in his works. It is a wonder that the reverend gentleman can tolerate the sweet singer of Israel. David of Cal Mall was a greater sinner than Bobby (if Scotland.

....... I An official intimation has been made that Judge Perronet Tholllll3o/1 Inns resigned his office of judge of Ne. II circuit, and that his resignation has been accepted by the Lord Chancellor. No. 6 circuit includes courts at Liverpool, Ormskirk, S . Helene, ISouthport, and Widnes, with jurisdiction in Admiralty !and Bankruptcy in Liverpool, and the last sittings of hit ! honour will be at St. Helens on the 2011, Liverpool en ! the 21st, and Widnes on the 22n1. Thomas Perronet Edward Thompson lA the son of the late General Perronet rhompoon, better known as Colonel Thompson, M.P. for Bradford in the days of the Corn Law agitation. General Thompson was a pithy and pregnant writer on the Free Trade vile of the agitation, unit wrote a well-known popular pamphlet in the form of a Corn Law Catechism." The present Judge Thomp- son is seventy-sin ware of age. Ile was educated at the Grammar School, Beverley, and at 1.1:111.1.5 College, Cambridge, where he took the degree of M.A. in 1838. Ile was milest to the Bar in 1838, and went on the Northern Circuit. lla practised at the List Riding Smsions, and was Resonslerof Scarborough from J.uarat to March, 1872, when he was appointed joint judge of Icircuit No. 8, in succession to Judge J. K. Blair. The other judge et the time was hesitant Wheeler, who was afterwards appointed judge of the 3larylebone County Curt, and he was summated here by the present Judge Judge Thotnpson lea J.P. for Lancashire, his teAldence heiria Dudtow Orange, Wavertree. lie is not ' unknown in it,B Bunting field, and he still occasionally Irides to hounds. The salary of a county court judge ta £1,500 a year, and we understand that a retiring judge after a certain length of service is entitled to a retiring pension. The appointtnent of a successor is practically in the hands of the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster (the Duke of Rutland), who makes a recommendation on the subject to the Lord Chancellor.

Dear Sir, -It so rarely occurs to me to see my remarks correctly rendered in print, (though possibly the fault lies with myself), that I gladly welcome an , exception to the general rule, and beg to express my acknowledgment, with thanks, of the excellent report of my speech, at the Earletnown Eisteddfod, ! which appeared in your issue a last satorday. , venture toothier to congratulate you upon the fact ! that you apparently possess a reporter who is at once intelligent and thoroughly master of Ms pro- fession. About four weeks ago he, feel- ing unwell, went to spend a few days with his . father, but he became so ill that it was impossible to remove him to his own residence, and he gradually became weaker and died. Mr. Linaker was the eldest won of Mr. Henry Linaker, of Prodsham and was 42 'we'll-known of age. He served his articles with the , well-known firm of Means. It was stated by Mr. Ileywood that the two 1 prisoners lived together RA man and wife, and that, on January 2nd the deceased child was bent at ; Cheadle, Staffordshire. They stopped at Cheadle for about a week and then went on to Crewe and Wid- I nes, the child being persistently neglected, as the prison- ers were repeatedly drunk. When they went out bog- ging they took the baby, and another child (our years old, with them. In public houses at Widnes, they used the infant most recklessly, dropping it Ott the floor like a bundle of rags, and generally treating it in a manner I repugnant to the feelings of any mother or of any I Christian. Polling commenced yisterday morn- ! ing for the election of a member of Parliament far the Kennington Division of Lambeth, in noon of Mr. Gent- Davis, Conservative, resigned. The candidates were Mr. Mark Beaufoy, tiladstonian Liberal, and Mr. P. Beresford Hope, Conservative. Both were well supported, and a keen contest took place for the seat. There are 9,943 electors int the register, and only 8,012 voted at the last election, when Gent- ' Davis had a majority of 430. A large supply of . carriages was sent for the use of the candidates by their friends.—The Premier, Mr. W. 11. Smith, Mr. Wilfour, the nuke of Norfolk, the nuke of Portland, the Duke of kbercorn, the Duke of Wellington, the Marquis of Bath, Lord Csmpenlown, the Earl of Fife, Sir John Lubbock, and Lord Londeshorough, were amongst those wino lent carriages to Mr, Beresford Hope ; while Mr. Beaufoy had conveyanov from Mr. Gladstone, Lord Aberdeen, Lord noblest's., Mr. Spencer Balfour, and many others. , A large number of city men voted in the first two hours. The railway men's vote, which ion considerable item in the electorate, went at the last election to Mr. Gent. Davis, but [bonnie it was divided. On the other hand, , omnibus employ, who are also numerous, were. all Con- servatives. Many lady canvassersassisted on hothsides, and in mltlition to earriages several private fire engines wen; used.
